newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: Philippine bourse president Nanagas resigns.
newsitem.headline: Philippine bourse president Nanagas resigns.

text.p: The president of the Philippine Stock Exchange, Vitaliano Nanagas, has resigned from his post after just over five months in the job, bourse chairman Wilson Sy said on Saturday.

"Nanagas has resigned and the board has accepted his resignation and the members have ratified the board's action, Sy told reporters at a news conference on the sidelines of the bourse's annual general meeting.
Nanagas' resignation comes in the wake of market talk of intense rivalries within the bourse over tough reform measures to be implemented.
Last week, other key bourse officials, including the heads of the compliance and surveillance and listing departments, had resigned for reasons not yet clear.
On Friday, Nanagas downplayed the series of departures, saying they had left for "greener pastures".
Former compliance chief Tomas Tuazon also resigned early this year.
Nanagas, a former president of state-owned Philippine Deposit Insurance Corp and an ex-Citibank executive, joined the Philippine Stock Exchange in October last year.
In the same month, Philippine Stock Exchange (PSE) members voted in favour of key reforms aimed at making the market more transparent and seat-holders more accountable.
Members voted in favour of three propositions: one admitting additional two non-brokers to the PSE board of directors and the second providing for an annual audit of members' accounts.
The third, and most contentious, allowed the stock exchange's surveillance department to examine members' accounts without first clearing this with the board.
Another recent change that annoyed many of the bourse's 186 members was the abolition of a rule which forced companies making initial public offerings to allot a certain percentage to the brokers.

The allotments to brokers were meant to ensure a wider distribution to small investors but SEC officials said the provision was abused by brokers who just sat on the shares and bought it on their own account if the stock did well.
If it did not debut at an attractive price, the brokers would simply return the shares to the underwriter, they said.
The brokers firmly rejected the allegation saying they were hurt by the change in the IPO allotment rule because it implied they were abusing it.
